cards.front: dashboard.ts imports fetchTasks from './api'. How can a Vitest test make fetchTasks return fake tasks without editing dashboard.ts?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Call `vi.mock('./api', () => ({ fetchTasks: vi.fn() }))` in the test file. Vitest moves (hoists) `vi.mock` above the imports, so every module that imports `./api`, including the code under test, receives the fake exports. The path is relative to the test file. Then pick data per test with `vi.mocked(fetchTasks).mockResolvedValue([...])`; `vi.mocked` only adds mock typings for TypeScript.

## A worked example

```ts
import { expect, test, vi } from 'vitest'
import { fetchTasks } from './api'
import { countOpenTasks } from './dashboard'

vi.mock('./api', () => ({ fetchTasks: vi.fn() }))

test('counts only open tasks', async () => {
  vi.mocked(fetchTasks).mockResolvedValue([
    { id: 1, title: 'Buy milk', done: false },
    { id: 2, title: 'Pay rent', done: true },
  ])
  expect(await countOpenTasks()).toBe(1)
})
```

`vi.mock` takes effect before the imports even though it is written below them, so `countOpenTasks` calls the fake.

## Picture it another way

`vi.mock` is like changing a supplier on a restaurant's order sheet before the kitchen opens: every cook who orders from `./api` gets your stand-in goods, and no recipe changes.

## A common mistake

Reaching for `vi.mock` when a simpler seam exists. If the function can take the dependency as a parameter or prop, pass a `vi.fn()` instead. Module mocks are invisible in the code under test and easy to leave stale.

## Try a small exercise

A test file has const fakeFetch = vi.fn() on line 3 and vi.mock('./api', () => ({ fetchTasks: fakeFetch })) on line 4, and the code under test imports './api'. Why does it fail, and what is the fix?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`vi.mock` is hoisted above line 3**, so its factory runs when `./api` is first imported, before `fakeFetch` exists. Vitest reports an error saying there must be no top-level variables inside the factory. Fix: `const { fakeFetch } = vi.hoisted(() => ({ fakeFetch: vi.fn() }))`, which is hoisted too.

cards.front: A note editor saves a draft 500 ms after the last keystroke. How can a Vitest test check that without really waiting half a second?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Call `vi.useFakeTimers()` before the code schedules its timer. Vitest then swaps `setTimeout`, `setInterval`, `Date`, and similar APIs for a fake clock that only moves when you tell it to. ## A worked example

```ts
import { afterEach, beforeEach, expect, test, vi } from 'vitest'

afterEach(() => vi.useRealTimers())

test('saves once, 500 ms after the last call', () => {
  const save = vi.fn()
  const saveDraft = debounce(save, 500)
  saveDraft('b'); saveDraft('bu'); saveDraft('buy')
  vi.advanceTimersByTime(499)
  expect(save).not.toHaveBeenCalled()
  vi.advanceTimersByTime(1)
  expect(save).toHaveBeenCalledWith('buy')
})
```

The test runs in milliseconds and pins the exact boundary: nothing at 499 ms, one save at 500 ms.

Fake timers turn the test's clock into a hand-cranked one: nothing ticks by itself, and each `advanceTimersByTime` turns the crank by exactly that many milliseconds.

cards.front: A TaskList component loads tasks in an effect. Why does screen.getByText('Buy milk') fail right after render(), and which query should the test use?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The first render shows the loading state; the tasks arrive a moment later, when the promise resolves and state updates. `getBy…` queries look once, right now, and throw if nothing matches. `await screen.findByText('Buy milk')` retries until the element appears or 1000 ms (the default timeout) pass. So: `getBy` for what is on screen now, `findBy` for what will appear, `queryBy` to check something is absent.

## A worked example

```tsx
import { render, screen } from '@testing-library/react'
import { expect, test, vi } from 'vitest'
import { TaskList } from './TaskList'

test('shows tasks after loading', async () => {
  const loadTasks = vi.fn().mockResolvedValue([{ id: 1, title: 'Buy milk' }])
  render(<TaskList loadTasks={loadTasks} />)

  expect(screen.getByText('Loading…')).toBeInTheDocument()
  expect(await screen.findByText('Buy milk')).toBeInTheDocument()
  expect(screen.queryByText('Loading…')).not.toBeInTheDocument()
})
```

`toBeInTheDocument` comes from `@testing-library/jest-dom`, loaded once in a setup file.

cards.front: Why does user-event's await user.type(input, 'Buy milk') test a form more realistically than fireEvent.change(input, { target: { value: 'Buy milk' } })?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

```tsx
  await user.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: 'Add task' }))
  expect(onCreate).toHaveBeenCalledWith('Buy milk')
})
```

cards.front: Why should a Vitest API test start the server with server.listen(0) instead of a fixed port like 3000?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Port 0 asks the operating system for any free port. The test reads the real one from `server.address().port` and sends requests there. A fixed port collides with a dev server already on 3000, or with another test file running in parallel, and fails with `EADDRINUSE`. Start the server in `beforeAll`, close it in `afterAll`, and call it with `fetch`, the way real clients do.

## A worked example

```ts
import { afterAll, beforeAll, expect, test } from 'vitest'
import type { AddressInfo } from 'node:net'
import { createServer } from 'node:http'
import { app } from './app' // an Express app or any (req, res) handler

const server = createServer(app)
let baseUrl = ''
beforeAll(async () => {
  await new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.listen(0, '127.0.0.1', resolve))
  baseUrl = `http://127.0.0.1:${(server.address() as AddressInfo).port}`
})
afterAll(() => new Promise<void>((resolve) => server.close(() => resolve())))
test('GET /health returns 200', async () => {
  expect((await fetch(`${baseUrl}/health`)).status).toBe(200)
})
```

The request goes through the real HTTP stack: routing, headers, and status codes.

## Picture it another way

Port 0 is like asking a restaurant for "any free table" instead of insisting on table 3 every visit. You just read the table number off your ticket before ordering.

## A common mistake

Reading the port before `listen` has finished. Until the server is listening, `server.address()` returns `null`, so the base URL breaks. Await the `listen` callback in `beforeAll`, and close the server in `afterAll` so no open handle outlives the file.

## Try a small exercise

Two API test files both call app.listen(3000), and Vitest runs the files in parallel. One fails during startup. What error do you expect, and what is the fix?

**`EADDRINUSE` (address already in use)**: the second file tries to bind port 3000 while the first holds it. Listen on port 0 in each file and build the base URL from `server.address().port`, so every file gets its own free port.

cards.front: In the Chrome Network panel, which tabs of a selected request show what your page sent and what the server answered?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Select the request row and read its tabs. Headers shows the URL, method, status code, and the request and response headers. Payload shows the query string and the body your code sent (form data or JSON). Preview shows the response formatted, such as JSON as a tree; Response shows the raw body text. Timing shows where the time went. The Fetch/XHR filter hides images and scripts so your API calls stand out.

## A worked example

```js
const res = await fetch('/api/tasks', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ title: '  ' }),
});
console.log(res.status, await res.text());
// 422 {"error":"title is required"}
```
For this request, Payload would show the blank title your code sent, and Response would show the server's reason for the 422 even if the UI only says "Save failed".

## Picture it another way

A request is like a posted parcel. Headers is the shipping label (where it went and how it was handled), Payload is what you packed, and Response is the reply letter that came back.

## A common mistake

Trusting Preview when response.json() throws. Preview formats what it can; check Response for the raw text. If it starts with <!DOCTYPE, the server sent an HTML error page, and JSON.parse fails with "Unexpected token '<'".

## Try a small exercise

Your form shows "Save failed" and the Network row for POST /api/tasks has status 422. Which request tabs tell you why the server rejected it?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Response (or Preview), then Payload.** A 422 means the server understood the request but refused its content, and the body usually says why, e.g. `{"error":"title is required"}`. Payload then shows what your code actually sent, such as a title of only spaces.

cards.front: After a login form posts and the page redirects, the POST disappears from the Network panel. Which setting keeps it in the list?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Turn on Preserve log in the Network panel. Without it, the request list starts fresh on each page load, so a form POST followed by a redirect to /dashboard is gone before you can read it. // POST /login: set the session cookie, then redirect (Post/Redirect/Get)

```js
  res.writeHead(303, { Location: '/dashboard', 'Set-Cookie': 'sid=abc; HttpOnly; Path=/' });
  return res.end();
}
```

cards.front: What do the Network panel's Disable cache checkbox and throttling presets let you reproduce on a fast development machine?

## Plain English Disable cache makes requests skip the browser's HTTP cache, like a first-time visitor, and only applies while DevTools is open. No tasks yet.

cards.front: Why copy a failing request from the Network panel as cURL or fetch instead of retyping it by hand?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Copy as cURL (also Copy as fetch, fetch for Node.js, or PowerShell) turns the exact request the browser sent, including URL, method, headers and body, into a command you can rerun. Replaying it in a terminal and changing one thing at a time shows whether the server or the page is at fault, and gives a teammate an exact reproduction. The copy can include Cookie and Authorization headers, so treat it like a password.

## A worked example

```bash
# Copied from the Network panel, trimmed, then replayed
curl -i 'http://localhost:3000/api/tasks' \
  -H 'content-type: application/json' \
  --data-raw '{"title":"  "}'
# HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
# {"error":"title is required"}
```
Editing only the body to {"title":"Buy milk"} returned 201 Created, so the server rule works and the bug is in what the form sends.

## Picture it another way

It is a photocopy of the exact form that was submitted, rather than your memory of what someone probably wrote on it.

## A common mistake

Pasting the copied command into a ticket or chat unchanged. If it carries your session cookie or bearer token, anyone who reads it can act as you until that credential expires. Remove the cookie (Chrome copies it as a -b flag) and any Authorization header first.

A POST works from Postman but fails from your React page. How can the Network panel give you an exact command to compare with the Postman request?

**Copy the failing request as cURL and replay it.** If it also fails in the terminal, compare its headers and body with Postman's; a missing Content-Type or a renamed JSON field is common. If it succeeds there, the difference lives in the browser, such as CORS or cookies.

cards.front: A production error shows the stack frame "at n (index-4f2a.js:1:24)". What turns it back into your file, function and line?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

A source map. Bundlers such as Vite minify your code into long lines with short names, so raw stack frames point at a column in a bundle. A source map is a separate .map file that links those positions back to the original file, line and name. When DevTools can load it, Console stack traces, the Sources panel and breakpoints show your original code. Vite only generates production source maps if you set build.sourcemap.

## A worked example

```text
$ node app.min.js
    at n (app.min.js:1:24)
    at e (app.min.js:1:70)
$ node --enable-source-maps app.min.js
    at formatName (profile.js:2:15)
    at renderProfile (profile.js:5:17)
```
Same crash and same terser-minified bundle with a .map file beside it. Node's --enable-source-maps does what DevTools does for you: it maps each frame back to the original function name and line.

## Picture it another way

A source map is like the index that links each page of a printed, reformatted edition back to the page and line in the author's manuscript.

## A common mistake

Publishing .map files to every visitor without meaning to; they expose your original source. Vite's build.sourcemap: 'hidden' creates the maps without the sourceMappingURL comment, so you can upload them to an error tracker instead.

## Try a small exercise

You deploy a Vite app with default build settings, and a user's console shows "at e (index-9c1d.js:1:3120)". Why can't DevTools show your source code?

**No source map was generated.** Vite's build.sourcemap defaults to false, so the bundle has no .map file for DevTools to load. Set it to true (public maps) or 'hidden' (maps for an error tracker only), rebuild, and reproduce the error.

cards.front: Which DevTools breakpoint kinds help you find the code that sends a wrong request or changes an element, without knowing the file?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

An XHR/fetch breakpoint pauses when a request URL contains text you enter, on the line that sends it. A DOM change breakpoint on an element pauses on the code that changes its attributes, its children (subtree), or removes it. Event listener breakpoints pause in handlers for events like click. A logpoint prints values to the Console without pausing or editing your code, and exception breakpoints pause where an error is thrown.

## A worked example

```js
const filter = {}; // a caller forgot to set status
const params = new URLSearchParams({ status: filter.status });
console.log(String(params));
// status=undefined
fetch(`/api/tasks?${params}`);
```
An XHR/fetch breakpoint on "status=undefined" pauses on the fetch call, and the Call Stack shows which component built the filter without a status.

## Picture it another way

A line breakpoint is a guard at one door. A DOM or fetch breakpoint is an alarm on the valuable itself: it rings no matter which door the intruder used.

## A common mistake

Scattering console.log lines through many files to trace one value, then committing some by accident. A logpoint prints the same values without changing your source.

## Try a small exercise

A toast element keeps getting the class "hidden" added, and you cannot find the code that does it. Which breakpoint pauses on that code?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**A DOM change breakpoint on attribute modifications.** Select the toast in the Elements panel and break on attribute modifications. The next time any script changes its class attribute, DevTools pauses on that line, and the Call Stack shows who called it.

cards.front: Why can the Application panel list a session cookie that document.cookie in the Console does not print?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

The cookie was set with HttpOnly. HttpOnly cookies are sent with matching requests but hidden from page JavaScript: document.cookie leaves them out and cannot overwrite them. DevTools is not page JavaScript, so the Application panel's cookie table lists every cookie for the origin, with Domain, Path, Expires, HttpOnly, Secure and SameSite columns, and lets you edit or delete them. That table is where you check whether a login cookie exists.

## A worked example

```text
Set-Cookie: sid=abc123; HttpOnly; Path=/; SameSite=Lax
Set-Cookie: theme=dark; Path=/

document.cookie                 -> "theme=dark"
document.cookie = 'sid=hacked'  -> still "theme=dark"
Cookie header on fetch('/echo') -> sid=abc123; theme=dark
```
In Chrome, the page script could neither read nor replace sid, yet the browser still sent it to the server.

## Picture it another way

An HttpOnly cookie is a sealed envelope the courier carries on every trip. It always reaches the server, but your page script cannot open or swap it.

## A common mistake

Deciding "the login cookie is missing" because document.cookie does not show it, or trying to read the session token in JavaScript to build an Authorization header. With an HttpOnly session cookie the browser sends it for you.

## Try a small exercise

After login, console.log(document.cookie) prints an empty string, but API calls still succeed. Is the session cookie missing?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Probably not; it is most likely HttpOnly.** HttpOnly cookies are hidden from document.cookie but still sent on matching requests, which is why the API works. Confirm it in the Application panel's cookie table (HttpOnly checked) or in the request's Cookies tab in the Network panel.

cards.front: Your PWA keeps loading the previous deploy's JavaScript after a reload. What can the Application panel's service worker section do about it?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

It shows the service worker controlling the page and whether a newer one is waiting to activate. Update on reload installs and activates the latest worker on every load; Bypass for network sends requests straight to the network; Unregister removes the worker; and a waiting worker can be promoted with skipWaiting. A waiting worker means the new code is installed, but the old worker still controls the page.

## A worked example

```js
// sw.js: cache-first, so a cached copy always wins
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  event.respondWith(
    caches.match(event.request).then((hit) => hit ?? fetch(event.request)),
  );
});
```
With this worker a cached index.html keeps pointing at the old hashed bundle after a deploy. Bypass for network makes the page load from the server again while you debug.

## Picture it another way

The service worker is a receptionist answering calls from yesterday's notes. Until you replace the receptionist or route calls around them, nobody reaches the updated office.

## A common mistake

Pressing reload again and again and expecting the new worker to take over. During a refresh the old worker keeps control, so a waiting worker stays waiting until every tab using the old one closes, or skipWaiting runs.

## Try a small exercise

After your deploy, the Application panel shows a new service worker "waiting to activate" while the page still runs old code. What does that mean?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**The new worker is installed, but the old one still controls the page.** It activates when every tab using the old worker closes, or when skipWaiting runs (a DevTools link or your app's update prompt). While developing, turn on Update on reload so each reload uses the latest worker.

cards.front: What does Chrome's device mode simulate when you test a phone layout, and what can it not tell you?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Device mode sets a phone-sized viewport, device pixel ratio and user agent, emulates touch, and can throttle network and CPU. It is only a first approximation: your code still runs on your computer's CPU in desktop Chrome, so real-device speed, hardware quirks and other browsers such as Safari on iPhone go untested. For a real Android phone, use remote debugging through chrome://inspect.

## A worked example

```css
.toolbar { display: flex; gap: 8px; }
@media (max-width: 600px) {
  .toolbar { flex-direction: column; }
}
```
In Chrome at a narrow window width, getComputedStyle reported flex-direction: column; at 1200px it was row. Device mode is good for checks like this; whether taps and scrolling feel right on a cheap phone still needs the phone.

## Picture it another way

Device mode is a flight simulator: excellent for learning the controls and checking the instruments, but it cannot prove how the real aircraft handles in turbulence.

## A common mistake

Marking a bug "fixed on mobile" after checking only device mode. Browsers on iPhone generally use Apple's WebKit engine, not the Chrome engine running your emulation, and a phone's CPU differs from your laptop's even with throttling.

A menu bug happens only on a user's Android phone, and device mode looks fine. How can you open DevTools on the page running on that phone?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Use remote debugging.** Turn on Developer options and USB debugging on the phone, connect it by USB, open chrome://inspect#devices in desktop Chrome, and click Inspect under the phone's tab. You get Elements, Console and Network for the real device; port forwarding lets the phone open your localhost dev server.

cards.front: How do you make merging a pull request automatically close the GitHub issue it fixes?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Put a closing keyword and the issue number in the PR description, such as `Fixes #42` or `Closes #42`. GitHub links the PR to the issue and closes the issue when the PR is merged. The keywords are close, fix, and resolve (plus their -s and -d forms). It only works when the PR targets the default branch (usually `main`); a PR into a release branch closes nothing. A plain mention like `See #42` only cross-links.

## A worked example

```text
Add due dates to tasks

Fixes #42

What changed: nullable tasks.due_date column and a date input on the edit form.

How to test:
1. Edit a task, pick tomorrow, save.
2. Reload the page: the date is still shown.
```

Merging this PR into `main` closes issue #42 and lists the PR on the issue. The "How to test" steps let the reviewer check the change without guessing.

## Picture it another way

It works like writing the ticket number on a repair invoice with "fixes": when the invoice is paid (the PR is merged), the ticket is closed for you. A note saying "see ticket 42" is only a reference and closes nothing.

## A common mistake

Writing `Fixes #42, #43` and expecting both issues to close. GitHub wants the keyword before each reference: `Fixes #42, fixes #43`. The other common miss is a PR that targets a non-default branch, where the keywords are ignored.

Your PR into `main` says: "Working on #88 and #91; fixes #88". After it is merged, which of the two issues does GitHub close?

cards.front: When should you open a GitHub pull request as a draft, and what does draft status prevent?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Open a draft when the work is not ready to merge but you want CI to run or a teammate to check the direction early. A draft pull request cannot be merged, and code owners are not automatically asked to review it. When it is finished and you have read your own diff, mark it **Ready for review**; that requests code-owner reviews and tells everyone it is complete. You can turn a PR back into a draft at any time.

## A worked example

```bash
# API part is done, the empty-state UI is not
gh pr create --draft --title "Task list: empty and error states" \
  --body "API done. Still to do: empty-state UI."

# later, after reading your own diff on GitHub
gh pr ready
```

`gh pr create --draft` and `gh pr ready` are the GitHub CLI versions of the Draft option and the Ready for review button.

## Picture it another way

A draft PR is like a document with "DRAFT" stamped across it: colleagues can comment on the direction, but nobody files it as final until you remove the stamp yourself.

## A common mistake

Opening a normal PR for half-finished work and writing "WIP, do not merge" in the title. Reviewers are requested right away, and someone can still click merge. Draft status is enforced by GitHub; a title is only a request.

## Try a small exercise

Your PR's API change is done, but the form still has a known bug. You want CI results and a quick opinion on the API shape today. How should you open the PR?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**As a draft pull request.** CI can run and you can ask one teammate for an early look, while GitHub blocks merging and does not auto-request code owners. Say in the description what is unfinished (the form bug), then mark it Ready for review once it is fixed and you have read your own diff.

cards.front: A reviewer leaves six comments on your pull request. How do you respond so their second review is quick?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Answer every comment with one of three things: the change you made and its commit ("Renamed in 4f2c1a9"), a short reason you disagree, or a follow-up issue for out-of-scope ideas. If they used GitHub's suggested-change feature, apply it with Commit suggestion (or batch several into one commit). Then re-request their review. Let the reviewer resolve threads where they asked a question, so nothing is closed before they agree.

## A worked example

```text
Reviewer: `d` is not a clear name.
You:      Renamed to `dueDate` in 4f2c1a9.

Reviewer: Should this endpoint also accept PUT?
You:      Kept PATCH only: the form sends partial updates.

Reviewer: This list should be paginated too.
You:      Agreed, but it is out of scope here. Opened #57.
```

Each reply points to a commit, a reason, or a follow-up issue, so the reviewer can check it in seconds instead of re-reading the whole diff.

## Picture it another way

It is like replying to an inspector's checklist: next to each item you write "fixed, see photo", "not needed because…", or "booked for next week". Any item left blank has to be inspected again from scratch.

## A common mistake

Pushing one big "address review" commit without replying to anything. The reviewer then has to work out which comments you handled, which you skipped, and which you disagreed with, so the second review takes as long as the first.

## Try a small exercise

A reviewer suggests replacing your 8-line date-formatting helper with a date library. You think the helper is fine for this PR. What reply would you leave?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Disagree briefly, give the reason, offer a way forward.** For example: "I kept the helper: it is 8 lines, tested, and only used by this screen. If we add more date logic I am happy to move to a library in a follow-up (#61)." Leave the thread open so the reviewer can resolve it once they agree.

cards.front: What does GitHub's "Squash and merge" put on `main`, and why can `git branch -d` then refuse to delete your local feature branch?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Squash and merge combines all of the PR's commits into one new commit on `main`. Your branch's original commits never become part of `main`'s history. `git branch -d` only deletes a branch that is merged into its upstream (or, with no upstream, into the current branch), so once the remote branch is deleted and pruned, Git finds those commits nowhere and says "not fully merged". After checking the PR is merged, use `git branch -D`.

## A worked example

```bash
# GitHub squash-merged PR #12 and deleted the remote branch
git switch main
git fetch --prune
git branch -d feature
# error: the branch 'feature' is not fully merged
git branch -D feature   # fine: the PR shows as merged
```

Reproduced with a local bare remote. While `origin/feature` still existed, `-d` deleted the branch with a warning; after the remote branch was deleted and pruned, it refused as shown.

## Picture it another way

It is like retyping a notebook of drafts onto one clean page in the official file. The content is there, but the notebook pages are not, so a clerk checking "is every notebook page filed?" says no.

## A common mistake

Squash-merging a huge PR full of unrelated changes. It lands as one commit, so `git bisect` or `git revert` later can only point at the whole bundle. Squashing works best when each PR is already one focused change.

## Try a small exercise

Your team squash-merges PRs and GitHub deletes merged branches. A 7-commit PR is merged. How many new commits does `main` get, and after `git fetch --prune`, will `git branch -d` delete the branch?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**One commit, and no.** Squash and merge creates a single new commit holding the PR's combined changes. The 7 original commits are in neither `main`'s history nor a remote-tracking branch any more, so `git branch -d` reports "not fully merged". Confirm the PR is merged on GitHub, then use `git branch -D`.

cards.front: Your PR branch is behind `main`. What is the difference between merging `main` into it and rebasing it onto `main`?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Merging `main` into your branch keeps your commits unchanged and adds one merge commit, so a normal `git push` works and anyone else on the branch is unaffected. Rebasing replays your commits on top of `main` as new commits with new hashes: the history is linear, but you must push with `--force-with-lease`, and anyone who already pulled the old commits now has copies that no longer match. Rebase branches only you push to; merge when others push to it too.

## A worked example

```bash
git switch feature
git merge main       # "feature work" keeps its hash 39cb84f
git log --oneline --graph
# *   ad62c83 Merge branch 'main' into feature
# |\
# | * d5754c8 main moves
# * | 39cb84f feature work
# |/
# * c6dbfef init

# same starting point, rebased instead:
git rebase main      # "feature work" becomes 779e845
```

Run both ways from the same state: the merge kept the commit's hash, the rebase created a new commit.

## Picture it another way

Merging is stapling today's updates to your report with a note "brought up to date here". Rebasing is rewriting the report as if you had started today: tidier, but anyone holding a copy of the old version now has one that does not match yours.

## A common mistake

Rebasing a branch a teammate has also pushed to, then force-pushing. Their commits can vanish from the branch and their local copy diverges. Check `git log origin/feature` for commits that are not yours first, or merge `main` instead.

## Try a small exercise

You and a teammate both push to `feature/export`. It is 20 commits behind `main`, and CI needs the latest `main`. Should you merge `main` in or rebase, and why?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Merge `main` into it.** Merging leaves the commits both of you already have untouched and adds a single merge commit, so a plain `git push` works and your teammate can simply pull. Rebasing would rewrite commits your teammate already has and require a force-push that can drop their work.

cards.front: A merged PR broke production. How do you undo its merge commit on `main` with `git revert`, and why is `-m 1` needed?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Run `git revert -m 1 <merge-sha>` and push. A merge commit has two parents; `-m 1` tells Git to keep parent 1 (the `main` side) and undo what the merged branch added. Without it Git stops with "is a merge but no -m option was given". The revert is a new commit, so nobody has to force-push or rewrite history. On GitHub, the Revert button on a merged PR does the same thing by opening a new PR.

## A worked example

```bash
git revert -m 1 133a21c --no-edit
# [main 7651b29] Revert "Merge pull request #7 from export-csv"
ls
# a.txt
# readme.txt          (export.js is gone)

# later: merge the same branch again
git merge export-csv
# Already up to date.
```

cards.front: `npm install dayjs` changed both `package.json` and `package-lock.json`. What does each file record, and why must both go into your pull request?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

`package.json` records the range you accept (`"dayjs": "^1.11.13"`); `package-lock.json` records the exact version of every installed package, including dependencies of dependencies. CI and deploy builds run `npm ci`, which installs exactly the lockfile, deletes `node_modules` first, never writes either file, and fails if the two disagree. So commit both: without the lock change CI fails, and the lock diff shows reviewers exactly which versions changed.

## A worked example

```bash
# "dayjs": "1.11.13" was added to package.json by hand; the lock was not updated
npm ci
# npm error `npm ci` can only install packages when your package.json
#   and package-lock.json or npm-shrinkwrap.json are in sync. Please
#   update your lock file with `npm install` before continuing.
# npm error Missing: dayjs@1.11.13 from lock file

npm install   # updates package-lock.json; commit it with package.json
```

Run with npm 10 (the error is one long line, wrapped here). The failed `npm ci` left the lockfile unchanged.

## Picture it another way

package.json is the recipe ("flour, any 1.x bag") and the lockfile is the exact receipt from the last shop. `npm ci` buys only what the receipt lists, so every cook ends up with the same items. `npm install` also follows the receipt and writes a new one only when the recipe changes, such as a new ingredient.

## A common mistake

Switching CI to `npm install` because `npm ci` failed. That hides an out-of-date lockfile, and CI then builds a dependency tree nobody reviewed. Run `npm install` locally, commit `package-lock.json`, and keep `npm ci` in CI.

## Try a small exercise

`package.json` has `"ms": "^2.1.2"`, the committed lockfile has ms 2.1.2, and ms 2.1.3 is now published. Which version does CI's `npm ci` install, and which does a teammate's fresh `npm install`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**2.1.2 for both.** `npm ci` installs only what the lockfile says. `npm install` also follows the lockfile while it still satisfies `package.json`, so the `^` range alone does not upgrade anything. The version moves only when someone runs `npm update ms` (or `npm install ms@latest`), which rewrites the lockfile, and that diff should be reviewed like code.

cards.front: In a Vite app, what happens to `import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL` during `vite build`, and who can read its value?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Vite replaces it with the literal value at build time, so the string ends up in the JavaScript bundle that every visitor downloads. Only variables prefixed `VITE_` are exposed this way; others, like `DATABASE_URL`, are `undefined` in client code. Two consequences: anything in a `VITE_` variable is public, so never put a secret there, and changing the value on the host later does nothing until you rebuild.

## A worked example

```js
// .env: VITE_API_URL=https://api.example.com
//       DATABASE_URL=postgres://user:pw@db/app
console.log(import.meta.env.VITE_API_URL);
console.log(import.meta.env.DATABASE_URL);

// dist/assets/index-*.js after `vite build` (minify off):
// console.log("https://api.example.com");
// console.log(void 0);
```

Built with Vite 8: the URL is a plain string in the shipped file, and the unprefixed variable was not exposed.

## Picture it another way

A `VITE_` variable is like text printed on a flyer before it is handed out: every reader can see it, and editing your notes afterwards does not change the flyers already printed. Only a reprint (a rebuild) updates them.

## A common mistake

Putting a payment or AI provider secret in `VITE_STRIPE_SECRET` because "it is in .env, not in the code". The build copies it into the bundle anyway. Secrets stay on a server; the browser calls your API, and the API uses the secret.

## Try a small exercise

A Vite app's `.env` defines `VITE_MAPS_KEY` and `API_SECRET`. After `vite build`, which of these reach the browser bundle: `VITE_MAPS_KEY`, `API_SECRET`, `import.meta.env.MODE`?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**`VITE_MAPS_KEY` and `MODE`.** `VITE_`-prefixed variables and built-ins like `MODE` (`"production"` for `vite build`) are replaced with literal strings. `API_SECRET` has no prefix, so `import.meta.env.API_SECRET` is `undefined` in client code. A key in the bundle must be one designed to be public.

cards.front: A React Router app opens `/notes/42` fine by clicking a link, but reloading that URL on the static host gives 404. Why, and what fixes it?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

Clicking a link changes the URL inside the browser without asking the server. Reloading asks the server for `/notes/42`, and a static host has no file at that path, so it answers 404. Add a fallback rewrite that serves `index.html` with status 200 for paths that are not real files; the app loads and the router renders note 42. Real files such as `/assets/*.js` must still be served as themselves.

## A worked example

```text
# Netlify: public/_redirects (Vite copies it into dist/)
/*    /index.html    200

# Scratch Node server over the same dist/ folder:
# no fallback:    GET /notes/42 -> 404
# with fallback:  GET /notes/42 -> 200 text/html (index.html)
```

Netlify does not rewrite a path where a real file exists, so built JS still loads. Other hosts have the same idea under other names (Vercel `rewrites`, nginx `try_files`).

## Picture it another way

It is like a building with one reception desk: whatever office number a visitor asks for, the front door sends them to reception (index.html), and reception walks them to the right room (the router). Without that rule the door says "no such office".

## A common mistake

Using a redirect to `/` instead of a 200 rewrite. The address bar changes to `/`, so the user lands on the home page and loses the note they reloaded. A rewrite keeps the URL and serves index.html's content.

## Try a small exercise

Fix a Netlify rule `/*  /  302` that sends every reload of `/notes/42` to the home page, so the note page still opens after a reload.

<!-- recall:solution -->

**Use a 200 rewrite to index.html: `/*  /index.html  200`.** A 302 is a redirect: the browser's URL changes to `/`, so the router renders the home page. A 200 rewrite serves index.html's content while the address bar keeps `/notes/42`, so React Router renders the note.

cards.front: You need to rename `users.name` to `full_name`. Why is one migration plus one code deploy risky, and what sequence is safe?
cards.back:
<!-- recall:teaching:v1 -->

## Plain English

During a deploy, old and new code run side by side, and a rollback brings old code back, so every schema change must work with both. Expand, then contract: (1) a migration adds `full_name`, run before the new code; (2) deploy code that writes both columns but still reads `name`; (3) backfill `full_name` from `name`; (4) switch reads to `full_name`; (5) in a later release, stop writing `name` and drop it.

## A worked example

```python
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL)")
old_insert = "INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (?)"  # old code, still running

db.execute("ALTER TABLE users RENAME COLUMN name TO full_name")
db.execute(old_insert, ("Grace",))
# sqlite3.OperationalError: table users has no column named name
```

With the expand step instead (`ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN full_name TEXT`), the same old insert kept working. PostgreSQL breaks the same way after a one-step rename.

## Picture it another way

It is like moving a shop: open the new address first, keep the old one open with a sign pointing to the new one, and close it only once customers have switched. Closing the old shop the day you open the new one strands people mid-trip.

## A common mistake

Running migrations after the new code already serves traffic. For a few minutes the new code queries a column that does not exist yet and returns 500s. Make the migration a separate deploy step that finishes before the new version takes requests.

## Try a small exercise

After adding `users.full_name` and deploying code that writes both columns, a teammate switches reads to `full_name` right away. Existing users now show a blank name. Why, and which step was skipped?

<!-- recall:solution -->

**The backfill.** A newly added column is NULL in every existing row; only new writes fill it. Copy the old values once no old code is still writing: `UPDATE users SET full_name = name WHERE full_name IS NULL`. Check that no NULLs remain, then switch reads to `full_name`.
